items.title: Stand up the identity directory with every grant rooted in a person
items.summary: The standalone identity directory: sign-in through the platform's own Rauthy fork, two upstream providers linked to one person, a signed authoritative identity, and the standalone screen journey, all installed against one PostgreSQL database. It is the root every later grant in the platform hangs from.

provenance.context: The identity platform statement (docs/design/identity/STATEMENT-2026-09-22.md) and IDENTITY-001; the cluster and its five briefs reached main in 55933549.

items.notes: The briefs build in order: DIRECTORY-002 before 003, 003 before 004 and 005. Each card runs through the board (brief_card, then card_build_v3).

items.title: Build the secrets broker so agents hold handles, never credentials
items.summary: A broker that keeps credentials behind handles: the door swaps a handle for the credential at use, the token revolver is the first consumer, and rotation and sealing happen without any agent ever seeing a secret.

provenance.context: The secrets cluster (docs/design/secrets) and its two briefs, written to ADR-001 and ADR-002.

items.title: Move the Rauthy fork onto the next hardened upstream release
items.summary: Rebase the platform's own Rauthy fork (ADR-009) onto the next upstream release that upstream tags as a release and whose changelog carries security or hardening fixes. Our commits stay on top of the upstream tag, unsquashed and unaltered; the pin moves to the rebased head; the fork builds and passes its own suite; the standalone install comes up from the rebased build against the existing database with no migration by hand; the provider-link behaviour of DIRECTORY-004 still holds.

provenance.context: Written ahead of its trigger from the Lys board card of the same name. Upstream was still v0.36.2 on 2026-09-23 and the fork is pinned to that exact version. The trigger is a fact recorded in the pull request (the upstream tag, its commit, its changelog entry), never a judgement.

items.notes: The card is built only when the trigger is met. It needs DIRECTORY-004 (the provider link commit the rebase must carry) and DIRECTORY-002 (the standalone install it must prove) landed first. If the rebase cannot carry a fork commit cleanly the card stops and reports the conflicting upstream commit rather than rewriting ours. Nothing in Cambium or Aion changes; no production node is touched; Tom's three acts stay Tom's.

items.title: Rewrite the decision quotes as plain statements in the team's words
items.summary: docs/design/decisions.json holds eight decisions (ADR-001 to ADR-008) whose quote field carries a person's words. Each quote becomes a plain statement of the decision in the team's words, with the decision, context, consequences and sources kept exactly as they are. ADR-009 and ADR-010 already read that way and are the pattern.

provenance.context: The canon rule of 24 September: repository canon holds no person's words and nothing personal. ADR-009 and ADR-010 (lys 586ef5f4) were written to it.

items.notes: Documents only. scripts/design/gate.sh must stay green: decisions.json validates against decisions.schema.json, which keeps the quote field required.

items.title: Give a session a home: its context record, kept byte for byte
items.summary: The home (identity platform steps 4 and 5): a running session's transcript captured into a home byte for byte, indexed for reading back, with the record of what the agent was given as well as what it did. Lanterns, translation and forks stand on it.

provenance.context: CONTEXT-001 (docs/design/identity/briefs) and the home cluster, landed on main with lys PR 8 (HOME-001, design.json, stories, checklist).

items.notes: Owned by Archie. The home cluster and HOME-001 landed on main with PR 8; the cached-index rule (lys-home Index::from_cached) is in that brief. Next: HOME-001 dispatched through the board.

items.title: Launch a session from its home on Claude Code through a kept template
items.summary: The home keeps a launch template per harness, starting with Claude Code, as an object named by its hash; lys-home render-launch turns a template and a session into the files a Claude Code launch needs and a printed launch line that resumes the rendered file by path, and records each render on the session so a stranger can tell which template a session was launched with.

provenance.quote: A session's home holds the pieces a new session is made from, the record, the canon and the handover, but nothing yet turns them into a running session on a given harness. Tom ruled at 16:00 on 22 September that the home keeps a preset template per harness which maps the pieces onto that harness, and that the mapping covers the MCP configuration, the environment variables, which secrets the session may read and which it may only use through a handle, what is appended to the system prompt, and where the prior conversation goes, delivered as files and runtime variables, command mappings in text, never a transcript converter. The change is a launch template for Claude Code, kept in the home as a versioned object beside the record, with its schema in docs/design/home, and a lys-home subcommand that reads a template and a session and writes the files a Claude Code launch needs. The files are the rendered JSONL under the chosen uuid and cwd as R4 renders it, an MCP configuration file, an environment file, an appended instructions file, and the launch line that resumes by path as R9 states. The template has named slots. The transcript slot is the one slot no template can map generically, so the template names how this harness fills it, and Claude Code fills it by resuming the rendered file by path. A secret named in the template is written as its handle and never as its value, and the launch line reads the value through the broker at start, which the secrets rows own. Every render of a template records the template hash, the session head hash and the written paths in a lys.harness_event entry on the session, so a stranger can tell which template a session was launched with. The subcommand prints a JSON report of hashes and paths and never prints transcript, block or body content, and a missing argument exits 2 naming it. Acceptance is that a fixture template and the recorded session from PROOF-RESUME render to a directory whose files match recorded hashes, that the printed launch line resumes the rendered path with the template's flags, that a template naming a secret writes only the handle and a search of the written files for the fixture value finds nothing, that rendering the same template and session twice yields identical hashes, and that a template with an unknown slot is refused by name. Not in scope are any harness other than Claude Code, launching on another machine, and the broker's own read. Filed by Archie on Tom's 16:00 ruling of 22 September 2026 and HOME-001 R4, R9 and R12 on lys main 0073b966, at 06:15 on 26 September 2026.
provenance.context: Filed on the ruling relayed at docs/design/identity/STATEMENT-2026-09-22.md line 181 and HOME-001 R4, R9 and R12, on lys main 0073b966; the card lead's answers on fork-on-resume, the fixture, use-only secrets, the unbuilt broker reader, the side-leaf event, the canon and the ruling's record are written into HOME-002.

items.notes: Further units, not written: Wire the secret slot's start-time read to the broker once SECRETS-002 lands; Launch from the template and capture the new session into the same home; Canon and handover slots in the launch template; Target profiles: sandbox and VM rendered from the template (P8); Launch on a second machine from a fetched home (stage 3); Templates for a second harness; manifold seat document consuming the printed launch line.

items.title: Record what a session was given at render: the lys.given context record
items.summary: At every launch-template render, lys-home appends a lys.given custom entry after the render event. It names each instruction document Claude Code will load for the session's working directory, and each file the render wrote, by path, byte length and SHA-256, in the load order measured on a named Claude Code version, with the environment variable names the template set and the kinds resolved and left unlisted, and never a document's content. Two subcommands list those records and check a file on disk against one by hash. This is step 4's context record: what a session was given, unsigned and unencrypted, shaped as hashes so that signing and encryption can be added later.

provenance.quote: Step 4 is what a session was given, not only what it did. When Claude Code starts a session it reads instruction documents the person did not type: the CLAUDE.md chain from the working directory upward, the user's own CLAUDE.md, the memory index the seat loads, the appended instructions file the launch template writes, the MCP configuration, and the names of the environment variables set for it. Today the launch template's render event records the template hash, the session head hash and the written paths, and nothing records which of those documents the session was given, in what versions and order. This card records that as the context record: at render, the template subcommand resolves the documents Claude Code will load for the rendered session's working directory and the home's own files it wrote, reads each one, and appends to the session, after the render event, a lys.given custom entry listing every document in the order the harness reads them, each as its path, its byte length and its SHA-256, with the harness name and version the order was measured on, and never a document's content. The resolution is measured, not assumed: the brief names the Claude Code version on this Mac and the order it loads instruction files in, from its own behaviour, and the proof document records that measurement. A lys-home subcommand lists a session's given records with their documents, and a second checks a listed document against a file on disk by hash, saying matches or differs and never printing either. The record is unsigned and the content is not encrypted: signing is stage 6 and comes when asked for, and encryption at rest is a stage 3 precondition card; the given entry names hashes only, so both can be added later without changing what is recorded. Acceptance is that rendering the fixture template for a fixture working directory holding a CLAUDE.md and a memory index appends a lys.given entry after the render event whose documents are those files plus the written appended instructions and MCP configuration, in the measured order, with lengths and hashes that match the files; that rendering twice gives two given entries whose document lists are identical; that changing one byte of the fixture CLAUDE.md changes exactly that document's hash in the next given entry; that the check subcommand says matches for the recorded file and differs after the change; that the given entry and the listing hold no document content, checked by a search for a fixture sentence; and that one real session render on this Mac is recorded in the proof document as hashes, counts and paths only. Not in scope: signing or anchoring the record, which is stage 6; encryption at rest; recording documents a session reads later by its own tools; harnesses other than Claude Code. This card stands on the launch template card, ct98Wv-2, and is built on main after it lands. Filed by Archie on his 22 September 2026 statement in lys that step 4 is what the agent was given, Tom's 16:00 22 September 2026 template ruling that every render is a receipted event, his 16:27 ruling that signing comes when asked for, and home DESIGN P7 and P8 at lys main 0073b966, on 26 September 2026.
provenance.context: A Cambium card on the home cluster, standing on the launch template card ct98Wv-2; the lead's answers settled the environment names member, the kinds member, what identical document lists mean, the order within one directory, that files reaching the request by @-import or from .claude/rules are recorded, given-check's exit status, and that the render's entry names @-imports and .claude/rules as unlisted kinds while a second entry at the first request records what reached the model.

items.notes: Renumbered from the HOME-002 it was written as, since the launch template took HOME-002 and RM-006 first; built on the launch template branch (RM-006, lys PR 14) and lands after it. Built on lys main after ct98Wv-2 lands. Further units, not written: Record settings.json in the given entry; Record SessionStart hook output in the given entry; Record plugin skill and agent listings in the given entry; Record output styles in the given entry; Record what reached the model, @-imports and .claude/rules included, in a second lys.given entry at the first request from the HOME-001 proxy's capture.

items.title: Light a lantern in the home and recall it by note and by point
items.summary: Stage 5 of the home: a lantern is a note plus a point in a session, lit on purpose as a lys.lantern custom entry at the session's head, whose note grows only by lys.lantern_epilogue entries. Three lys-home subcommands light one, add an epilogue, and recall lanterns by an exact case-folded phrase of their note or epilogues, or by session and entry id, printing the lantern and its epilogues and never the transcript around the point. A lantern lives in the home and is never rendered into a Claude Code resume file.

provenance.quote: A lantern is a note plus a point in a transcript, declared on purpose at a moment of completion, success or learning, never automatically; it is what a later session, or a fork, walks back to. The home holds sessions in Pi's grammar and adds nothing to that grammar, so a lantern is a lys.lantern custom entry appended at the session's head, carrying the point it marks as the id of an existing entry in that session, the note as written, who lit it and when. The point may be any entry on the session's tree, not only the head, so a lantern can mark a place the session has already moved past. A note is append-only and grows: an epilogue is a lys.lantern_epilogue custom entry naming the lantern's own entry id and carrying the further words, so a lantern's story is its entry followed by its epilogues in order, and nothing is ever rewritten. A lys-home subcommand lights one: it takes the home, the session, the entry id of the point and the note, refuses by name a point that is not an entry of that session and an empty note, appends the entry, and prints a JSON report of the lantern's id, session, point and time. A second subcommand adds an epilogue to a named lantern. A third recalls: by note, listing every lantern in the home whose note or epilogues contain the given words, exact and case-folded, no vectors; and by point, listing every lantern that marks a given session and entry id. Each listing row is the lantern's id, session, point, lit-by, lit-at, note, and its epilogues, and never a line of the transcript around the point. A lantern is not rendered into a Claude Code resume file; it lives in the home. Acceptance is that on a fixture session a lantern lit at a past entry is recalled by a word of its note and by its point; that two lanterns on the same point are both recalled by point; that an epilogue is recalled with its lantern, after it, and recall by a word that appears only in the epilogue finds the lantern; that lighting at an unknown entry id and lighting with an empty note are each refused by name; that after lighting, the session file's earlier bytes are unchanged and the head is the lantern entry; that the rendered Claude Code file of that session contains no lantern line; and that no listing prints transcript content, checked by a search for a fixture message's text. Not in scope: the fork through a lantern, which is stage 5b and its own card; resonance, whispers, vectors and any ranking; dimming by code churn; Norn's tables; Cambium's screen. Filed by Archie on Tom's definition of 8 August 2026 that a lantern is a note plus a pathway back, declared deliberately, notes append-only, his roadmap stage 5 of 22 September 2026, and home DESIGN P2 and P7 at lys main 0073b966, on 26 September 2026.
provenance.context: The stage 5 lantern card on the Lys board, surveyed against lys main 0073b966; the lead of the home card answered the survey's open questions (phrase matching, the P7 and CN3 exception, held sessions, blank notes and epilogues, epilogue authorship, unknown points in recall, lanterns as points) and HOME-004 carries those answers.

items.notes: HOME-004 is the first unit. Further units, not yet written: Stage 5b: fork through a lantern (cut at its point and seed a new session); Lit-by from a directory identity rather than a declared name; Lighting from a live session under capture (the door's proxy or harness hook); Cambium's lantern screen; Recall by resonance and vectors, with ranking and churn dimming.

items.title: Make the Claude Code render byte-deterministic for the same session head and version
items.summary: Two renders of the same session head give different bytes whenever the context path holds an entry whose id is not uuid-shaped, which the importer writes for every tool record with more than one result: the render draws a fresh random uuid for each. The render derives those uuids from the record instead (UUIDv5 over a fixed lys namespace, the session id and the entry id with its role), a fixture carrying the defect is pinned by hash in a test and in PROOF-RESUME.md, and the resume is re-measured on the Claude Code installed on this Mac. A rendered file can then be told by its hash, a receipted render event can name what was written, and the launch template's identical-hash acceptance has ground to stand on.

provenance.quote: The Claude Code render in crates/lys-home walks a session's context path and writes the JSONL file that Claude Code 2.1.282 on this Mac resumes by path, as HOME-001 R4 and R9 landed it on lys main 0073b966. Rendering the same session twice does not give the same bytes today when a tool record on the path holds more than one result, which the translation card's survey found on 26 September 2026 while reading the render for the Codex rollout, and the launch template card's acceptance that rendering the same template and session twice yields identical hashes stands on the render being deterministic. A render of the same session head with the same lys-home version is one function of the record and must give the same bytes every time, so a reader can tell a rendered file by its hash and a receipted render event can name what was written. The change finds why two renders of a multi-result tool record differ, names that cause in the proof document, and makes the render byte-deterministic for the same session head and the same version without changing what the rendered file holds or how Claude Code resumes it. Where the cause is an order that the record does not fix, the render takes the order the record gives, entry order then part order, and never a map's or a set's order; where the cause is a fresh id or a clock, the value is derived from the record's own ids and stamps as the fork and launch cards derive theirs. Acceptance is that a fixture session holding a tool record with more than one result renders twice to files of equal SHA-256; that the fixture from PROOF-RESUME renders twice to equal hashes; that a recorded fixture hash in the proof document matches the render at the landed commit; that the rendered file still resumes in Claude Code 2.1.282 on this Mac, recorded in the proof document as before; and that the proof document names the cause found. Not in scope: any change to the importer, the record's shape, or the rendered file's content beyond the determinism, and any harness other than Claude Code. Filed by Archie on the translation card's survey of 26 September 2026, on Tom's rule of 16 September 2026 to find the underlying cause, and on lys main 0073b966.
provenance.context: Filed on the translation card's survey, which found the nondeterminism while reading the render for the Codex rollout; surveyed on lys main 0073b966. The lead's answers settled the Claude Code version the resume is measured on (the one installed when the proof runs, as `claude --version` prints it, with the rendered records' version field left at 2.1.281) and that this card defines the id derivation the fork and launch cards follow; a follow-up card ruled that the derived uuid is salted with the session id.

items.notes: Renumbered from the HOME-002 and RM-006 it was written as, since the launch template took HOME-002 and RM-006, the context record HOME-003 and RM-007, and the lanterns HOME-004 and RM-008 first. Stands on HOME-001's render (R4) and CLI (R9), already on main at 0073b966, so no roadmap dependency is written. Further units, not written: Make the Claude Code import deterministic for the same transcript; Render tool parts from the stored block so a round trip adds only the new turn; Move the render's default Claude Code version off 2.1.281. ADR-016 is proposed and binds the fork and launch cards' id derivation.

items.title: Fork a session from a lantern's point and launch the child
items.summary: Stage 5b of the home: lys-home fork takes a lantern id, resolves it to the session it was lit in, cuts that session's chain at the last assistant message at or before the lantern's point, and writes a child session holding the parent's own lines with its ancestry on both sides (the header's parentSession, a lys.forked_from entry in the child, a lys.fork entry at the parent's head), adding nothing to the block store and rewriting nothing in the parent. A user-message point is carried as a seed prompt the child's render writes beside the rendered file and the launch line passes as the first prompt. The child renders and launches through the launch template, measured on the installed Claude Code version.

provenance.quote: A lantern is a pathway back to a conversation with the self that lit it, and Claude Code resumes a session only from its end. This brief delivers the fork that makes the pathway: a new session in the home cut from the parent's chain at a lantern's point, carrying its ancestry on both sides, adding nothing to the block store and rewriting nothing in the parent, then rendered and launched like any session. It is stage 5b of the home and stands on the lantern card's lys.lantern entry (the design's solution and ADR-012).
provenance.context: The stage 5b fork card on the Lys board, surveyed against lys main after the lantern card; the lead's answers settled that the fork stands on the lantern card and is built on the main it lands on, that the child launches through the launch template's line, that the copied lines are the parent's own bytes with the same hashes and the block store unchanged, that lys.forked_from is the first entry the fork writes, that parentSession carries the parent file's path as Pi reads it, that a user-message point is carried as a seed and never dropped, that a lantern resolves to its lit-in session (lit_in) with the older-record rule until the lantern card records it, that a lantern before any assistant message is refused nothing_to_fork, and that non-text parts of a carried message are counted, never refused. HOME-006 carries those answers.

items.notes: Renumbered from the HOME-002 it was written as; HOME-006 follows the lantern card (HOME-004, RM-008) and the launch template (HOME-002, RM-006), both on main, and after the render card (HOME-007), which took RM-009, ADR-016, C31 to C35, S18, S19 and CN9. Further units, not written: lit_in written by the light act (the lantern card's next round); a fork given tools, a lens or a briefing on what changed since the point; leases, budgets and kill rules; harnesses other than Claude Code.

items.title: State the rendered-uuid rule with its test vector in RECORD.md, pin it by a test, amend the launch card and decide ADR-016
items.summary: A rendered Claude Code record's uuid for an entry id that is not uuid-shaped is derived from the home session's own id and the entry id together, so two sessions with the same id rendered into one Claude Code directory never collide. HOME-007 landed that derivation in the code; this item writes the contract: the one rule and a test vector in RECORD.md, a named test that reads the vector so the document and the render cannot drift, the launch card amended to name the rule in place of its SHA-256-of-the-entry-id-alone derivation, and ADR-016 moved to decided. No rendered byte changes.

provenance.quote:
The render's record uuid for an entry whose id is not uuid-shaped is the SHA-256 of the entry id alone, so an id like e1 renders to the same uuid in every session, and two sessions rendered into one Claude Code directory can collide. The uuid is derived from the session id and the entry id together, one rule stated in RECORD.md with its test vector, and the launch card's derivation is amended to name it. Every existing render test keeps passing with the new vector; a fixture with the same entry id in two sessions renders two different uuids. Found by Waffles reviewing lys PR 14. Not in scope: ids that are already uuid-shaped, which pass through unchanged.

Corrections from Waffles' cross-review of the brief HOME-008 at 50135be on 26 September 2026 at 19:32, carried into the words for the re-fire. C1: R1 and RECORD.md name the salt as the home session's own id, the one render.rs passes at its one call site, and never the render target's session id that the rendered file's sessionId carries, matching ADR-016. C2: an acceptance line fails when HOME-008 is duplicated on any branch, for example git log --all on docs/design/home/briefs/HOME-008.json naming only this brief's commits. C3: R2's drift check is a command run on a scratch copy with its expected result stated, exactly one test fails and it is named record_md_states_the_rendered_uuid_rule_with_the_vector_the_render_derives, not a hand edit written up in the dev record. C4, from the lead's own check: git diff 1756688 50135be on docs/design/decisions.json is empty, so the brief left ADR-016 proposed; the brief moves ADR-016 to decided as its round one answered, and the dev record shows that diff, whose only lines are ADR-016's status and the ledger's updated date.
provenance.context: Found reviewing lys PR 14, before HOME-007 salted the derivation; re-fired with the corrections of a cross-review of the earlier HOME-008 brief. The lead answered that the card ships the contract only, with no change to render.rs.

items.notes: Stands on HOME-007 R1, which landed the salted derivation, so render.rs does not change. Further units, not written: none.

items.title: Translate a session imported from Claude Code into a Codex rollout with a loss account
items.summary: Stage 4b of the home: lys-home translate-codex renders a session imported from Claude Code as a Codex 0.156.0 rollout in the shape Codex writes for its own threads, carrying every text part, tool call and tool result whole, readable thinking as text and sidechains as marked text, with a JSON loss account beside it of what was kept, changed and lost by entry id and hash, a lys.translation side leaf on the session, and a resume on Codex 0.156.0 measured in a scratch Codex home. The Codex thread is a fork of the session, never the same session.

provenance.quote:
Translation is designed and not proved: the lantern work measured three session formats and left the converter out, so the first translation is one named pair, one session, and an account of what was kept, changed and lost, and nothing above it assumes it. The pair is Claude Code to Codex, the pair the lantern work measured: Codex's own importer of Claude Code files is the recorded baseline, a compaction and not a copy, dropping thinking, sidechains and meta records and clipping tool calls and results, and Tom ruled on 5 September 2026 that we improve on it and do not adopt it. This card renders a home session that was imported from Claude Code as a Codex rollout that Codex 0.156.0 on this Mac resumes, with a loss account beside it. A lys-home subcommand takes the home, the session, a target directory and the Codex version it renders for, walks the context path as the Claude Code render does, and writes a rollout file in the shape that version of Codex writes and reads for its own threads, measured from the files Codex writes here and never assumed from the June checkout; every text part is carried whole, every tool call and result is carried whole as Codex's own items for a call and its output and never as a truncated note, and readable thinking is carried as text while opaque blocks are dropped and named by hash in the loss account, as P3 rules for another provider. The rendered thread announces itself in band as a translated context with the source session id and the render's template hash, following the marker precedent, so the fork can never mistake itself for the original. The loss account is written beside the rollout as JSON and lists, by entry id and block hash, what was kept, what changed shape and how, and what was lost and why: sidechains, harness events, lanterns and other lys entries, and any block kind Codex has no item for. The report is JSON with the rollout path, entry and block counts, the loss counts and the account's path, never content. Acceptance is that a fixture session imported from a fixture Claude Code file renders to a rollout whose items match a recorded fixture rollout for Codex 0.156.0 apart from ids and timestamps; that the loss account names every dropped block by hash with a reason and every changed block with its before and after kinds; that a session with a thinking block from another provider renders it as text and the account says so; that a tool result longer than Codex's importer clips is carried whole; that rendering to an existing path is refused by path and writes nothing; that the rendered rollout is resumed by Codex 0.156.0 on this Mac and answers from its content, recorded in a proof document with hashes, counts and paths only; and that the Claude Code render of the same session is unchanged, checked by hash. Not in scope: Codex to Claude Code, which does not exist in any tree here; adopting or calling Codex's importer; Pi or any third harness; launching Codex through the launch template, which is that template's next version. Filed by Archie on Tom's roadmap stage 4b of 22 September 2026 at 14:45, his 5 September 2026 ruling on the Codex converter, the lantern design's session-formats measurement, and home DESIGN P1, P3 and P7 at lys main 0073b966, on 26 September 2026.

Corrections from Waffles' cross-review of the brief at db97e15 on 26 September 2026 at 19:24, carried into the words for the re-fire on lys main 1756688. C1: R5 counts as changed, naming the field in how, every part that lost or changed a field: a tool_use that loses its caller field, a one-item text array result written as a plain string, and an assistant turn whose model, usage and stop reason go nowhere; none of these is kept. C2: the session_meta line does not copy model_provider, source, thread_source or history_mode from the Codex fixture, values the Claude session never held; each is either named as a changed entry-level line with before none and after the key, or left out when Codex resumes without it. C3: every R2 refusal names the act that answers it, and the acceptance lines assert those words: UnmeasuredCodexVersion says render for 0.156.0 or card a measurement of the new version; BlockNotStored says re-import the source file; UnknownTimeZone and UnnamedTimeZone say set TZ to an IANA name; Exists says choose another --out. C4: R1's fixture recording and R10's resume spend Codex model requests, and the Codex account Chippy and Gypsy use has been at its usage limit since 26 September and resets on 30 September; the brief names the account it uses, checks at its start that the account can make requests, gives the refusal words and the act that answers them, and bounds R1's record-again loop with a stated count. C5: the thread id is record_uuid of the session head, so each head makes a new Codex thread and its turns never come home once Codex continues it; the brief states plainly that the Codex thread is a fork of the session and not the same session, and that the durable link back is the account and the side leaf, not the marker text, which a Codex compaction can erase. C6: every requirement names its command and its exact result, for example cargo test -p lys-home --test codex_translation with the test's name printing 1 passed and 0 failed, and a grep -c on PROOF-TRANSLATE.md for each field it must hold; this covers every R1 line, R4 to R8, and R10's proof checks. The brief is written at lys main 1756688 or later, so its id allocates past HOME-007 and its ledger carries every decision main carries.

This card is re-fired at main on 26 September after its second run, 24724e9e, published a rewrite at 37a47f6 whose base was main 1756688 but whose ids all clash with open brief branches. The lead ruled at 20:48 that DIRECTORY-002 goes first because it fired first and keeps ADR-021, and that this card takes the next free ids under her 20:31 rule (next id after main's highest and every open brief branch's), checked before the fire.

items.title: Build the secrets broker in lys from a baseline, a reviewed contract and counted code rows
items.summary: SECRETS-003, beside SECRETS-002 and without editing it: a documents-only baseline recorded from source, a contract with key custody and an adversarial review by a second commit author before any code, and code rows in crates/lys-secrets, ordered R3, then R4, then R5 to R8, that deliver SECRETS-002's R1 to R9 with counted acceptance legs, each with a runnable command and its exact result, a tested presenter check, anchored criterion searches, red-first tests, an injected clock and refusals that name their act, re-costed hours per row, and DIRECTORY-002, DIRECTORY-003 and DIRECTORY-006 R1 to R4 as blockers with runnable checks. The broker's home in lys is ADR-019, decided, amending ADR-001's placement of the broker; the lease is a broker record bounded by the lys-identity grant's window (ADR-020).

provenance.quote:
The unlanded draft IDENTITY-003 under docs/design/identity/briefs does not land; that directory sits outside the gate. The broker's brief on main is the secrets cluster: docs/design/secrets/briefs/SECRETS-001.json (done) and SECRETS-002.json, R1 to R9 with SEC_ identifiers, anchored to ADR-001 (secrets sit behind a handle the door swaps for the credential), ADR-002 (the token revolver is the first consumer), ADR-003 and ADR-004.

This brief is SECRETS-003, a brief of its own beside SECRETS-002, so what has landed stays stable; SECRETS-002 is not edited. It adds, in docs/design/secrets/, what the draft carries and main lacks: a documents-only baseline row recording from source the revolver's next-account call site, every consumer of the account pool file, every credential path into a seat today classed as the login exception, a proxied credential or neither, and what lys/delegation/v1 and the sealed envelope can carry for a handle, a lease and a sealed record, by file and line; a contract row before any code stating the invariant, the handle, the lease with its atomic use step and retry outcome, the cancellation rule, the SpiceDB relations and the audit line fields, with an adversarial review recording every attack tried (a replayed or forged handle, a use spent or counted twice, an admitted call outliving the rule, a credential in a log, a sealed key read, a stale SpiceDB answer) and the clause defeating each; counted acceptance legs on every code row (each refusal leg, a forced race on a k-use lease admitting exactly k, a redaction canary with a positive control, kill and reopen at each append boundary, each in-flight outcome its own test); hours per row; dependencies on DIRECTORY-002, 003 and 006 blocking the code rows.

Settled on main, not reopened: the seat's own login reaches its process at spawn as the one named exception (R5); OAuth refresh and spend caps are in scope (R4, R9); every point it records open stays open.

Boundaries: documents only, no code; no credential value; lys-core and its published formats unchanged, a signed lease format only as a new version alongside with its own adversarial review; no engine structural; no row dispatched before the lead's review; the gate is scripts/design/gate.sh.

Ask the lead, do not decide: whether the broker lives in lys (the draft's crates/lys-secrets) or in the cambium door SECRETS-002 names, which CN4 leaves open; whether the lease is a broker record or a signed format; whether the draft's hours stand. The brief records each as an open question with both readings.

The lead read the brief published at 4babcfe on 26 September and found the baseline R1 sound and holes in R2 to R8; every one of these corrections goes in, and R1 stays in this brief.

Blockers a build can act on. SECRETS-003.json carries depends_on [] while DIRECTORY-006 uses that field: name the DIRECTORY-006 requirements this brief waits on as R1 to R4 of 006, never the whole of 006, whose R6 waits on 005; give each blocker a check a stranger can run, a file, a command or a landed commit to look for.

The order of the code rows. R3 to R8 do not block on each other today, yet R4 edits R3's lib.rs, R6 and R7 use R4's revocation states, and R5 and R8 build on R4's proxy: state the order R3, then R4, then R5 to R8, in each row's own Blocked by.

The CONFORMANCE 3.2 and 3.4 review blocks only at brief level: put it in R4's own Blocked by.

Key custody. Nobody holds the store's encryption key: add a key-custody section to CONTRACT.md saying which key, where it is kept, how the store is unlocked and how the key is rotated; add R3 checks that the key is not in the store directory and that opening the store without it is refused by name.

Canaries on disk. Every canary check also searches every file under the test's store and log directories, expecting zero matches, with a positive control that plants the value and finds it.

The audit line and the handle. The audit line carries a handle id or digest only, never the raw handle, since the transparency log can be read and replayed; the handle is stored hashed; the canary plants a handle value. The Handle section says how the proxy authenticates whoever presents a handle.

Points R2 keeps open that the code rows must settle: the audit line's signer and schema, and how a sealed record is bound to its name and owner, since sealed_envelope.rs:182 has an empty AAD; R3's store gains a refusal check for ciphertext swapped between two entries. Either the contract states a broker-internal shape, reviewed adversarially, or those rows stay blocked and say so.

The delegation's time window. ADR-020 says the signed delegation keeps it, v1 has no window, and DIRECTORY-006 R1 puts it in the lys-identity grant: name the grant's window as the limit, amend ADR-020 to match, and list which criteria still wait on it.

ADR-001 says the broker is built in Rust inside the door and ADR-019 moves it into lys with supersedes []: record ADR-019 as amending ADR-001 and fix design.json:54. ADR-001 is Tom's decision; the lead puts the move to him herself, and the brief says the amendment waits on his word.

SEC_REVOKE_FRESHNESS has one fixed expected behaviour: R4 calls the landed DIRECTORY-006 permission check and asserts that behaviour and zero forwarded calls.

SEC3_OAUTH_RACE asserts that the provider sees exactly one refresh for three simultaneous calls.

The criterion mapping is searchable: "the row's report maps each criterion" names the report path, or the criterion ids sit in the test names so a search proves the mapping.

The canary scope is countable: say how logs are captured, a tracing subscriber in tests/support; keep every secret byte in one redacting type; enforce that with an ast-grep rule or a counting test.

File lists. R4 and R5 list crates/lys-secrets/Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock; tests/support/mod.rs is listed on every row whose test doubles live there.

Two different identities are checked as two different commit authors in git log, and SEC3_STORE_RACE states its total case count.

Roadmap row, ruled by the lead on 26 September 2026 at 21:07 after the re-fire ad15e87e published at 36cddea with RM-011, which HOME-008 already holds on brief/home/5898fcb0, and after translate took RM-012 at 20:52 under her 20:31 rule (the next id after main's highest and every open brief branch's): SECRETS-003's roadmap row is RM-013, appended after RM-012, and its brief and ledger name RM-013 wherever the rewrite at 36cddea said RM-011. Checked by Archie at 21:07 against main 1756688 and every open brief branch (brief/directory/7e9506d8, brief/home/24724e9e, 31aa723f, 5898fcb0, 7d3f3efb, c322f3e6, d388a9f7, de72f0a4, e35a7157, brief/secrets/604f95d0 and ad15e87e), none of which holds RM-012 or RM-013. ADR-019 and ADR-020 stay as the rewrite has them, ADR-019 proposed as an amendment to ADR-001 until Tom's word. The rewrite at 36cddea is otherwise the text to carry: its answers to the fifteen corrections stand and the author reopens none of the rounds of runs 604f95d0 and ad15e87e.

The lead read the re-fire published at 36cddea on 26 September at 21:13 and found R1 and R2 sound, C6 present (R2 and R3 keep only the SHA-256 digest, proved by SEC3_STORE_CANARY), and thirteen holes in R3 to R8; every one of these goes in before her tick, and the line numbers name SECRETS-003.json at 36cddea.

K2, the presenter check is tested. SEC3_PROXY_REFUSALS (:158) gains three legs, a handle presented unsigned, a signature by a key other than the bound identity's, and a valid signed presentation replayed on a new call, with its asserted count raised; R6, R7 and R8 (:234, :268, :303) gain the same legs. R2's acceptance (:78) also requires the contract to state the unsigned refusal, the freshness limit on a presentation's timestamp, and that the check uses lys-core's verify_attestation_by_signer, since plain verify_attestation never compares the signer (attestation/mod.rs:51-63).

K3, anchored searches. rg -c 's002_r1_ac1' also matches ac10, ac11 and ac12, so R4's criterion 1 would pass once R3 lands: every such search is anchored, for example rg -c 'fn \w*s002_r1_ac1(_|\b)' (:120, :166, :204, :240, :274, :308, :350).

K4, test names are snake_case, so a name holding SEC3_STORE_REFUSALS fails clippy -D warnings and the lint is not silenced: every search looks for the lower-case form, sec3_store_refusals, sec_revoke_freshness and the rest (:121, :164, :167, :205, :241, :275, :309).

K5, SEC3_SECRET_SCOPE lets only store.rs read raw secret bytes (:117) and Zeroizing only in secret.rs, yet key_rotation.rs, handle.rs and audit.rs all need the bytes: either name every R3 file that does, or route all of them through store.rs.

K6, red first. Each code row's first commit adds its tests, and cargo test at that commit fails naming each leg.

K7, no wall clock. SEC3_PROXY_INFLIGHT's slow upstream double (:162) becomes a double held until the test releases it; the window and expiry legs (:111, :199, :200) use an injected clock, as DIRECTORY-006's GRANT_EXPIRY does; no sleeps.

K8, every refusal names the act that answers it and its leg asserts that act: StoreKeyMissing says supply the store key file at start, StoreKeyRetired says use the current key, every-account-rested says bring an account back, and so on through :109, :111, :113, :158, :198, :234, :268 and :303.

K9, every counted leg gets a runnable command and an exact expected result, for example cargo test -p lys-secrets --all-features --test store_leases sec3_store_ -- --include-ignored printing N passed, 0 failed, 0 ignored. R2's document checks (:76-86) either become heading or id searches with expected counts, or say plainly that the lead checks them by reading.

K10, "planted in the store" (:116 and the canary legs of R4 to R8) contradicts digest-only storage: the canary handle is issued through the broker and presented.

K11, a leg for R3's retry rule (:109): the same operation id returns the first outcome with the use count still 1, and the same operation id under a different handle or identity is refused.

K12, rollback. The sealed binding stops a swap between entries but not someone restoring an older ciphertext of the same entry: rollback joins the attack list (:85), and either a version or sequence is bound into the sealed prefix with a refusal leg at :111, or the contract records it out of scope.

K13, canary searches also look for lower- and upper-case hex and for standard and URL-safe base64 (:112, :114, :116 and the rest), so a hex-written key or a Basic auth header cannot pass.

K14, R2's handle clause (:78) sets at least 32 bytes from the OS secure random source, because an unsalted SHA-256 of a short handle can be brute-forced; the handle id is generated separately and never derived from the handle; one assertion checks that no audit line carries the handle's digest, which :82 forbids and nothing tested.

Three suggestions from the same review, not blockers, which the author takes or records as not taken with a reason: SEC3_STORE_KEY also searches the log directory; the contract covers audit-key rotation and what happens if the audit key is compromised; blocker check (a) checks each path separately.

The re-fire 18b96d68 was taken back before it published so these corrections ride with the RM-013 ruling in one run, at main 1756688. The tick still waits on Tom's word on ADR-019.
provenance.context: The secrets broker card on the Lys board: the lead's reviews of the SECRETS-003 drafts published at 4babcfe and at 36cddea, with the fifteen corrections to R2 to R8 carried as the rewrite at 36cddea answered them, the thirteen further corrections K2 to K14 to R3 to R8, and the ruling that this row is RM-013, surveyed against lys main at 1756688. The lead's answers: SECRETS-003 keeps ADR-019 (proposed, amending ADR-001, waiting on Tom's word) and ADR-020 (decided); R5's OAuth refusals gain the same three presenter legs as R4, R6, R7 and R8; a stale presentation gets its own refusal leg on the injected clock in every row that carries a presenter check, so R4 to R8 assert 10, 9, 8, 10 and 8 refusals; and a sequence is bound into the sealed prefix, so an older ciphertext of an entry restored in place is refused by name.

items.notes: Takes the next id after translate's RM-012; the id the rewrite at 36cddea carried is HOME-008's. Further units, not written: SECRETS-003 R1: BASELINE.md recorded from source; SECRETS-003 R2: CONTRACT.md with key custody, and the adversarial review by a second commit author; SECRETS-003 R3: store, redacting type, handles and leases in crates/lys-secrets; SECRETS-003 R4: proxy, rotation and cancellation rule; SECRETS-003 R5 to R8: OAuth refresh, login at spawn, sealed records, next account; A later Lys brief for the screen and API legs of SEC_USE_NOT_LEND, SEC_PEOPLE_ONLY and SEC_REVOKE_STATES; A lys-core sealed-envelope version with AAD beside v1, if the contract cannot bind a sealed record otherwise; Add ast-grep and clippy pedantic legs to .land/gates.sh for crates/lys-secrets; Audit-key rotation and the response to a compromised audit key.

items.title: Leave a signed audit receipt for every sign-in and permission change
items.summary: One audit receipt of IDENTITY-001's shared shape for every sign-in and every permission change: signed by the service that performed the operation and never by the party it is about, returned beside the signed event appended to the lys log in operation order, and checked offline by lys log verify receipt, which needs only the log and the service's public key and refuses a payload-commitment mismatch under the published CLI's one refusal class. DIRECTORY-007 carries it in five rows: the contract document, the receipt crate crates/lys-receipt, the CLI verifier, the sign-in and sign-in-refusal receipts the directory service emits, and the development-install proof with test receipts under a test key and a test tag. DIRECTORY-003 R2, DIRECTORY-004 ID001_LINK_AUDIT and DIRECTORY-006 GRANT_AUDIT keep emitting their receipts inside their own walls.

provenance.quote:
Every sign-in and every permission change on the platform leaves an audit receipt, and this card writes the brief for that receipt and the code that emits and verifies it. The receipt's shape is the shared contract IDENTITY-001 already names: a version, a stable operation id, the actor, the affected identity, the operation, a commitment to the payload, and the log coordinate where the record sits; the brief carries that contract as written and adds nothing to it without a lead's ruling. The operations that must emit one are a person signing in through Rauthy (success and refusal), a provider being linked to a person, a grant being given or taken away, an agent being provisioned, and an identity moving between lifecycle states; each receipt is signed by the service that performed the operation, never by the party it is about, because a claim must not be settable by the party being judged. Receipts append to the lys log in the order the operations happened, and a verifier given the log and the service's public key confirms each receipt's signature and its coordinate, and refuses by name a receipt whose payload commitment does not match the record it points at. The brief states what already stands on main and must not be reopened: the shared contract in IDENTITY-001, the audit-record wording in LIFECYCLE-STATES-2026-09-22.md, and the rule that Tom's three acts (publishing lys-anchor, generating a production key, emitting a receipt outside a test) stay his. Boundaries: no production key, no production anchor, test identities only, and no change to the products that call the service. Questions for the lead rather than the survey: whether a permission check that is merely answered (not changed) leaves a receipt, and where the verifier lives (the lys CLI or the directory service).

Under the lead's ruling of 26 September at 20:31 that a brief's ids are the next after main's highest and every open brief branch's, this brief is DIRECTORY-007 at docs/design/directory/briefs/DIRECTORY-007.json, its roadmap row is RM-015, appended after RM-014, which the DIRECTORY-002 re-fire 073049e0 holds, and any decision it records is numbered from ADR-024 upward, after ADR-023 on brief/home/9e701467. Checked by Archie at 22:34 against main 1756688 and every open brief branch, brief/home/31aa723f, 5898fcb0, 7d3f3efb, 9e701467, c322f3e6, d388a9f7, de72f0a4, e35a7157 and brief/secrets/309540a4, none of which holds DIRECTORY-007, RM-015 or ADR-024.
provenance.context: The audit receipt card on the Lys board, re-fired at main 1756688 on 26 September after run dc7fb926 was cancelled while writing and run 7bed2f5b ended failed at 23:16 when the author desk's account pool was exhausted; the automated brief author being down, the lead's word of 23:49 had each lead write the brief by hand from the card's words and every answer given. The lead's rulings of 22:56 settled the three open questions: W1 receipts are for changes only and answered checks go to step 2's separate access record (ADR-024); W2 the verifier lives in the lys CLI, offline (ADR-025); W3 a development install emits test receipts under a test key and a test tag (ADR-026). The settled answers A1 to A12 are carried in DIRECTORY-007: it defines the common receipt and replaces nothing (A1); the leaf is the signed event with the receipt beside it (A2); the encoding stays with IDENTITY-EVENTS.md (A3); Rauthy's own refusals are out of scope (A4); provisioning is the register transition and the grants (A5); grant receipts wait on the grant representation (A6); A8 corrects A7, in step 1 a first sign-in registers nobody (A8); the verifier keeps the published CLI's one refusal class with named pre-crypto refusals (A9); the lys release waits for ratification (A10); step 1 refuses exactly one kind of authenticated sign-in (A11); unlink and display-profile edits are inside the common receipt and the verifier enumerates no vocabulary (A12).

items.notes: Appended as RM-015 under the lead's ruling of 26 September at 20:31 that a brief's ids are the next after main's highest and every open brief branch's: RM-011 to RM-014 sit on other branches (RM-014 on the DIRECTORY-002 re-fire 073049e0) and are absent from this tree, so this file goes from RM-010 to RM-015 on purpose. ADR-019 to ADR-023 likewise sit on other branches, so the decisions here are ADR-024 to ADR-026. Development record: main corrected A7, since DIRECTORY-003 R1 has a first sign-in register nobody in step 1, so the first sign-in leaves a sign-in or refusal receipt and the administrator's register act leaves the register receipt (A8); every count a leg asserts (leaves per scenario, cases per tamper matrix, refusals per leg) was decided by rule in the brief, as the lead decided the E10 counts for the sibling briefs tonight. Depends on RM-001 because R2 to R5 wait on DIRECTORY-003's envelope and crates. Not written here, as later units: step 2's access record; the lys release carrying the verifier; grant receipt payloads (with DIRECTORY-006).

items.title: Carry the lead's rulings into the dependency install brief of the identity directory
items.summary: Carries DIRECTORY-002, row 02 of the identity directory that RM-001 owns and links, forward from RM-001 with the lead's rulings and nothing else: dark-only Rauthy client themes from the estate tokens with eight named gaps (ADR-021), exactly two managed clients beside Rauthy's built-in one, the container-backed identity targets declared test = false and run, linted first, only on their own identity leg of the landing gate, sibling unit-test files, and a check that the ledgers carry every entry main held. The brief keeps its id, its path and its four requirements; RM-001 keeps its link to it, unchanged.

provenance.quote:
The brief for this card already stands in the cluster: docs/design/directory/briefs/DIRECTORY-002.json and DIRECTORY-002.md, "Install the standalone service dependencies on one PostgreSQL database", Row 02 of IDENTITY-001 revision 5, on main. This card rewrites it in place with the lead's rulings E1 to E11 below and nothing else, keeping its id, its path and its four requirements. Keep its four requirements exactly: R1 package Rauthy, SpiceDB and one PostgreSQL database and install them for development; R2 prepare, configure and check the deployment from the lys CLI; R3 theme both Rauthy clients with Aion's vocabulary and each product's own accent (ADR-010: every product shares one design and keeps its own accent); R4 state what SpiceDB enforces in step 1 and hold to it. Keep its boundaries and verification as written except where E1 to E11 say otherwise, and change nothing else that the method (scripts/design/validate.py, check-coverage.py, render-cluster.py, run by scripts/design/gate.sh) does not require. Facts the brief already settles, which the survey must not reopen: PostgreSQL may live on one of the network devices and the host is confirmed with the operator before anything is installed; the install runs on a node the operator names (ADR-005) with test identities only; the Rauthy installed is the maintained fork (ADR-009) at its pin from Row 01; one PostgreSQL holds both Rauthy and SpiceDB. Nothing here is a production node, no production key is generated and no receipt is emitted outside a test; those three acts are Tom's. If the survey finds a sentence of DIRECTORY-002 open or contradicted by the repository as it stands, quote that sentence as a question for the lead rather than rewriting the brief around it. This card supersedes the archived board 2 twin "Install the three services on one PostgreSQL", whose sign-off carries over.

This card is re-fired at main on 26 September after its first run, 7e9506d8, published a rewrite of DIRECTORY-002 at 3fe22ceb on a base 22 commits behind main. E1 (round 1, answered by the lead, 26 September 16:02, as the published brief at 3fe22ceb records it). items.title: Start and check the pinned Rauthy in a demand gate leg
items.summary: One gate leg, cadence demand, declared in docs/design/project.json and in the directory cluster's gate. It starts the Rauthy image whose revision label equals the vendor/rauthy pin against a scratch PostgreSQL container, the Rauthy image by its local image ID and PostgreSQL by its digest reference, both read from DIRECTORY-002's deploy/identity/versions.json. It passes only when Rauthy answers ready and removes everything it made. It refuses by name when the runtime or an image is missing, and it lets no secret into its output, which a round-leg test proves. It closes the release row's missing Rauthy check; .land/gates.sh is not changed.

provenance.quote:
The Rauthy container that DIRECTORY-002 installs is started and checked by a gate leg declared in the lys design project file, and the leg runs on demand.

DIRECTORY-002 installs the maintained Rauthy, SpiceDB and one PostgreSQL database, but no gate leg starts the Rauthy container and checks it.
The release card holds that gap as a blocker.
This card adds one leg to the lys design project file on main 7b536253, with its cadence set to demand, so it runs when it is asked for and never in every round.
The land gate script is not changed.

The leg starts the Rauthy pinned in the vendor submodule in a container against a scratch PostgreSQL database, waits for its readiness answer, then stops it and removes everything it made.
It passes only when Rauthy answers ready.
When the container runtime or the image is missing, the leg refuses by name and says which one, and it never passes by skipping.
Its requirements name the tools it needs, the way the other legs do.
No secret reaches the leg's output, and a test searches that output for key and token material.

The acceptance lines are that the project file validates against the project schema with the new leg, that the leg passes on a machine with the runtime, and that it refuses by name on a machine without one.

items.title: Keep a Claude Code compaction beside its original with a lys.loss account, a listing that checks it, and the compact_boundary render
items.summary: Stage 4's first derived record. The importer maps both Claude Code compaction shapes, the current compact_boundary pair and the legacy summary record, into one Pi compaction entry that keeps what Claude Code kept, and appends after it a lys.loss entry naming by ids, counts and SHA-256s the span it summarised; the summarised entries stay on the tree and in the block store. lys-home compactions lists a session's compactions and checks every span entry and block; the Claude Code render writes a compaction as the compact_boundary pair, measured to resume on Claude Code 2.1.283; a proof records one real compacted session by counts and hashes.

provenance.quote:
A compaction is the first derived record, because the harness itself produces it: Claude Code writes a summary record and keeps everything before it in its own file, and the importer already turns that record into Pi's compaction entry with its summary and first kept entry. What the home does not yet say is what the compaction could not keep, and nothing yet proves, on a compacted session, that the original is all still there. This card adds both. When a compaction entry enters a session, on import of a Claude Code file that carries a summary record, the importer appends directly after it a lys.loss custom entry that points at the compaction by entry id and names what fell outside the kept range: the first and last entry id of the span it summarises, from the root or the previous compaction to the entry before the first kept one, and the counts of entries, messages, tool calls, tool results and blocks in that span with their bytes, and the tokensBefore the harness reported; it names entry ids and hashes and never a word of content. The summarised entries are not touched: they stay on the tree, their blocks stay in the store, and the context path is Pi's reading as today, the compaction first, then the kept entries. A lys-home subcommand lists a session's compactions: for each, the compaction entry, its loss entry, and a check that every entry in the summarised span is still readable by id and every block it references is still held, printed as a JSON report of ids, counts and hashes. A render for Claude Code writes the summary record and the kept entries as R4 does now, and never the loss entry, so the harness sees what it expects while the home keeps the whole. Acceptance is that a fixture Claude Code file with a summary record imports to a session whose compaction entry is followed by a loss entry naming that compaction, the span's first and last ids and counts that match the fixture; that every entry before the first kept one is still on the tree with its blocks present, checked by the listing; that the context path is the compaction followed by the kept entries and nothing from the span; that the rendered file holds the summary record and the kept entries and no loss line; that importing the same fixture twice into two homes gives byte-identical loss entries apart from ids and timestamps; that a summary record whose first kept entry is not on record is refused by uuid as the importer refuses an unknown parent today; and that one real compacted Claude Code session is imported on this Mac and its listing recorded in a proof document as counts and hashes only. Not in scope: the home compacting a session itself; translation, which is stage 4b and its own card; changing what Claude Code writes; the handover letter, which is HOME-001 R12. Filed by Archie on Tom's roadmap stage 4 of 22 September 2026, a compaction is stored beside its original, points at it and says what it could not keep, the original never replaced, and on home DESIGN P1, P2 and P7 and HOME-001 R3 and R4 at lys main 0073b966, on 26 September 2026.

Ruling (Archie, lead, 27 September 2026 07:56, after run 5c15394f ended survey_malformed because the acceptance above is one sentence joined by semicolons, which a question cannot quote whole). These rulings settle the survey's questions, each in a sentence of its own. The importer handles both shapes Claude Code has written: the current compact_boundary pair and the legacy summary record. For a compact_boundary, the first kept entry is the entry named by compactMetadata.preservedMessages.anchorUuid when that field is present, and otherwise the entry after the boundary. For a legacy summary record, the first kept entry is the entry named by its leafUuid. A missing first kept entry is refused by uuid, as the acceptance says. A compact_boundary whose logicalParentUuid names no record in the file is not refused: it imports with the span ending at the last known entry, and the loss entry names that logicalParentUuid as unresolved, because 16 of 149 measured real boundaries carry one. The loss entry counts entry line bytes and block bytes separately. The loss entry names the SHA-256 of the span's first entry line, of its last entry line, and of the span's lines concatenated in file order. The fixture carries one compact_boundary pair and one legacy summary record, each sized so its span holds at least one of every counted kind. Two imports of the same fixture into two homes give loss entries that are byte-identical apart from the ids and timestamps the home assigns, which the test masks by name. The real session in the proof is a current compact_boundary session from this Mac's Claude Code, read only; the 2.0.53 file in ~/.claude.bak2 may be imported as well but does not satisfy that line.
provenance.context: The compaction card on the Lys board, filed on the context roadmap's stage 4 and home DESIGN P1, P2 and P7 and HOME-001 R3 and R4, with the card lead's ruling after an earlier run ended survey_malformed. The survey's open questions were answered by the card lead: the kept range begins at the earliest preserved uuid; the render writes the compact_boundary pair measured on 2.1.283; the card replaces the self-pointing mapping and the listing reports older homes unaccounted; the isCompactSummary record becomes the compaction's summary and block only; the compaction takes that record's place on the chain with no exception to HOME-001 R3 and the loss entry hangs off it; and the span's hashes are over path lines only, with side leaves and sidechain entries counted by number. HOME-008 carries those answers.

items.title: Judge certificate admission at an instant its caller names, and take the sleep out of its expiry test
items.summary: RecognisedCertificate gains admit_at, judging a submission at an instant its caller names on lys-core's existing verify_certificate_chain_at; admit keeps its signature and calls it with the present, so a live request is judged as before. an_expired_certificate_is_refused stops sleeping 2.1 seconds and asserts admitted inside the one-second window and NotAdmitted two seconds past issuance at explicit instants, so the suite no longer pays a wait on every run or depends on a host's load. lys-core is not changed.

provenance.quote:
The test an_expired_certificate_is_refused in crates/lys-anchor/src/admission/certificate_tests.rs issues a certificate valid for one second and then sleeps 2.1 seconds so that the admission policy sees it expired. That wait is a clock. Under load the sleep proves nothing about the code, on a loaded host it is the kind of wait that makes a suite slow, and the suite pays it on every run. Tom's word of 27 September 2026, relayed by Waffles in the pipeline channel: tests must not take this long and things must not fail under load; a test that waits on the clock is a defect in the code, not a flake. The crate lys-core already carries verify_certificate_chain_at, which takes the instant to judge against, and its API is frozen at 0.2.0 and is not changed here.

The rule to meet: an admission policy judges at an instant its caller names. RecognisedCertificate gains admit_at, taking the statement, the asserted credential and the instant, built on verify_certificate_chain_at; admit keeps its signature and calls admit_at with the present, so nothing that admits a live request changes. The test issues the same one-second certificate and calls admit_at twice with no sleep: at an instant inside the validity window it asserts admitted, and at an instant two seconds past issuance it asserts NotAdmitted. The positive control stays, the refusal is still the only check that tells a chain verification that consults the window from one that does not, and the test runs in milliseconds.

Acceptance: the sleep is gone and both assertions stand on explicit instants; a grep for thread::sleep and tokio::time::sleep across crates/lys-anchor prints nothing; every other admission test is unchanged and green; no timeout is raised and no test is split; the change is one commit on the card branch. Keep to the method (scripts/design/validate.py, check-coverage.py, render-cluster.py, run by scripts/design/gate.sh). The cluster is lys-anchor, new under docs/design, holding only this card's documents; the brief id is the first for that cluster's prefix, and the roadmap row and any decision take the next free id after main's highest and every open brief/* and draft/* branch's, checked with git ls-remote immediately before writing. Not in scope: how notAfter is truncated at issuance, lys-core's public API, or any other test in the workspace. If a sentence here is open or contradicted by the repository as it stands, the survey quotes it whole as a question for the lead. Filed by Archie on 27 September 2026 on lys main 7b53625.

items.title: Run every test binary in the gate's test leg with --no-fail-fast
items.summary: The gate's test leg stops at the first failing test binary, so a red round hides every failure after the first. One commit changes it to `cargo test --workspace --all-features --no-fail-fast` in docs/design/project.json, the directory, home, secrets and lys-gate design.json gate arrays and .land/gates.sh, and, by the lead's rulings, in CLAUDE.md's 'Gates before any commit' block (so .land/gates.sh still matches it exactly) and CI's test step (which gains the one flag only; its missing --all-features is a finding left unchanged). Nothing else in any gate moves. Proved by a grep over the declared legs that prints 0, the green gate round's '$ command' line for the tests leg, one gate round over a local scratch branch with a planted failing test in crates/lys that never reaches origin, and a proof document that names that round's log by path, SHA-256 and counts.

provenance.quote:
The lys gate's test leg stops at the first failing test binary. Five files declare it as `cargo test --workspace --all-features`: docs/design/project.json (the project gate), docs/design/directory/design.json, docs/design/home/design.json and docs/design/secrets/design.json (the cluster gates), and .land/gates.sh (the landing hook). A run that fails in one crate reports nothing about the binaries and crates after it, so a gate can go red for one reason while hiding others.

This card changes that leg in all five files to `cargo test --workspace --all-features --no-fail-fast`, in one commit. Every test binary then runs, every failure is reported in the one gate run, and the leg still exits non-zero if any test fails. Nothing else in the gate changes: the other legs, their order and their requirements stay exactly as they are. No timeout is raised and no test is split.

It is done when all five files declare the new command and scripts/design/gate.sh stays green. A check over docs/design/project.json, every docs/design/*/design.json and .land/gates.sh must show that no test leg there still runs `cargo test --workspace --all-features` without --no-fail-fast. The ledger that runs the gate recognises a battery by the text "cargo test" in a leg's command, so each changed leg must still be classed as a battery, shown in the gate log. One gate round over a scratch branch that adds a single failing test in one crate must show in its log that failure together with every other test binary measured; that branch is never landed. The briefs under docs/design/*/briefs and the release documents quote cargo commands as acceptance text or instructions, not as gate legs, and this card does not change them.

Keep to the method (scripts/design/validate.py, check-coverage.py and render-cluster.py, run by scripts/design/gate.sh), and render any cluster whose design.json changes. items.title: Revoke a certificate by appending a leaf and fold the live set from the log
items.summary: Builds DP26 for certificates: revoking is one leaf appended to an append-only certificate log through lys-log-store, never a deletion or rewrite, and the live set is folded from the log. A revoked certificate fails revocation-aware verification, which takes the size N and a tolerance as explicit inputs with no default and names the revocation leaf, while its log proofs, its issuance record and the attestations logged before its revocation still verify, and an attestation by a certificate not revoked needs no log entry. A certificate carries one claim and is the revocable unit, only its issuing authority's key revokes it, a revocation is permanent, and a revocation naming a certificate with no earlier issuance is refused (ADR-039). The code lives in lys-identity; lys-core and every published format are unchanged, and lys ca verify keeps its meaning with help saying it does not check revocation. It stands beside DIRECTORY-006 R4 and leaves C25 open. DIRECTORY-013 carries it in seven rows.

provenance.quote: Write the brief for this card in the directory cluster (docs/design/directory/briefs, next free id), building lys decision DP26, ruled and not built: revoking is an append to the log, and the live set of certificates is folded from it; the LeafStore exposes no delete and no rewrite, so revocation is a leaf, never a removal. Done when a revoked certificate fails verification and its history still verifies. Hold to DIRECTORY-006 R4 (revocation, inherited expiry and current permission decisions) and to lys-log-store's append-only contract. Keep to the method (scripts/design/validate.py, check-coverage.py, render-cluster.py, run by scripts/design/gate.sh). items.title: Prove the block and template stores' second put writes nothing without waiting on the clock
items.summary: The two lys-home store gates that sleep 20 ms before a second put instead pin the shard directory's and the stored file's modification times to a fixed past instant, read them back, and assert after the second put that both are unchanged and the shard's entry count is the same. No sleep; the store write paths, every other test and canon.rs's millis_now are untouched.

provenance.quote:
Two tests in crates/lys-home sleep so that a file's modification time can tell a second put that wrote nothing from one that rewrote the same bytes: the_same_bytes_put_twice_occupy_one_block_and_the_second_put_writes_nothing in src/record/blocks_tests.rs and a_template_is_kept_once_under_its_hash_and_a_second_put_writes_nothing in src/record/templates_tests.rs, each sleeping 20 milliseconds before the second put. That wait is a clock. On a filesystem with coarse timestamps, or on a loaded host where the second put lands inside the same tick, the 20 milliseconds prove nothing, and the suite pays the wait on every run. Tom's word of 27 September 2026, relayed by Waffles in the pipeline channel: tests must not wait on the clock and must not fail under load; such a wait is a defect, not a flake.

The rule to meet: the proof that a second put writes nothing does not depend on elapsed time. Each test, before the second put, sets the stored file's modification time to a fixed instant well in the past with std::fs::File::set_modified, reads it back to confirm the instant took, and after the second put asserts the modification time is still exactly that instant and the directory count is unchanged. No sleep. The stores' write paths are not changed: they already write once by hash, and this card only makes the tests prove it without a clock.

Acceptance: both sleeps are gone; a grep for thread::sleep and tokio::time::sleep across crates/lys-home prints nothing; both tests keep every other assertion they have today; no timeout is raised and no test is split; the change is one commit on the card branch. Keep to the method (scripts/design/validate.py, check-coverage.py, render-cluster.py, run by scripts/design/gate.sh), in the home cluster; the brief id, roadmap row and any decision take the next free id after main's highest and every open brief/* and draft/* branch's, checked with git ls-remote immediately before writing. Not in scope: the block or template store's write path, any other test, or the canon's millis_now, which records a timestamp and waits on nothing. If a sentence here is open or contradicted by the repository as it stands, the survey quotes it whole as a question for the lead. Filed by Archie on 27 September 2026 on lys main 7b53625.
provenance.context: The words' sentence on the stored file's modification time is settled by the lead's answer: both the shard directory's and the stored file's modification times are pinned, read back and asserted unchanged, in the block test and in the template test, because the directory's modification time is what catches a temporary file created and deleted in the shard.

items.title: LanternData carries lit_in, the light act records it, recall reports it and the fork reads the typed field
items.summary: A lantern records the session it was lit in. LanternData gains an optional lit_in; the light act writes it as the id of the session at whose head it appends the lantern and prints it in its report; recall rows carry it beside point, note and lit_by, null for a lantern lit before it; and HOME-006's fork reads it through a narrower typed view in place of the raw-data stopgap, with L2 in both fork fixtures lit by the light act and only the records the light act cannot produce written by hand. A lantern with no lit_in stays an older record resolved by its holders (ADR-017), and a present lit_in that is not a session id is refused lit_in_not_a_session by the fork and by recall, never read as any session (ADR-046).

provenance.quote: The lantern's typed data does not carry lit_in and the light act does not record it, so HOME-006's fork reads lit_in from the entry's raw data as a stopgap and the fixtures write L2 by hand. This card makes the typed field the shape. LanternData gains lit_in, the session that held the point when the lantern was lit; the light act records it at the head of the session holding the point; recall reports it beside point, note and lit_by. The fork in HOME-006 reads the typed field and its hand-written fixtures light L2 with the light act instead. A lantern record without lit_in, or with a lit_in that is not a session id, is refused by name as it is today, never read as any session. Ordered after HOME-006 lands. Acceptance: a lantern lit with the light act recalls with lit_in equal to the lighting session; the fork's fixtures contain no hand-written lantern entry; the two lit_in refusals keep their tests; the existing lantern and fork tests keep passing; ADR, checklist and user story rows renumbered past HOME-006's.
